issues.legal_issue: A court may not impose a uniform buffer zone on future land acquisitions when the restriction is not tailored to the ecological circumstances and would broadly obstruct industrial development.
material_facts: The High Court directed that a one-kilometre green area be left from village limits whenever land was acquired for industrial, commercial, or other non-residential purposes.
The Supreme Court considered that the direction could prevent future land acquisition for industrial development and set it aside.
issues.conclusion: The general one-kilometre buffer-zone direction was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Sustainable development requires balancing industrial development with ecological preservation. Protective restrictions should respond to the carrying capacity and circumstances of the ecosystem concerned; the buffer zone upheld in M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, (1997) 3 SCC 715 was based on expert recommendations concerning particular lakes. Environmental protection is also supported by Articles 21, 48A and 51A(g) of the Constitution.

predicates.appeal_from_general_buffer_order: A party appealed from a court order imposing a general buffer-zone restriction.
predicates.buffer_order_applies_uniformly_to_future: The order applies the buffer-zone restriction uniformly to future land acquisitions rather than tailoring it to particular ecological circumstances.
predicates.buffer_order_would_obstruct_industrial_d: The restriction would obstruct land acquisition for industrial development.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns a uniformly applied buffer-zone order that would obstruct industrial development, the order is set aside as non-site-specific.

issues.legal_issue: Before acquiring land for development, the acquiring authority must assess the environmental consequences and avoid acquisitions that would gravely impair ecology and the environment.
material_facts: The proceeding concerned land acquired for development of an industrial area, including land alleged to serve grazing, agricultural, residential, or green-belt purposes.
The respondents raised concerns about environmental effects of industrial development, and the Court considered that development could affect ecology and the environment.
issues.conclusion: For future development acquisitions, the authority must properly assess the consequences and adverse environmental impact before acquisition and acquire land only where development will not gravely impair ecology and the environment.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied sustainable development: development and environmental protection must proceed together, and development must not exceed the ecosystem's carrying capacity. The principle is supported by Articles 21, 48A and 51A(g) of the Constitution and the precautionary principle recognized in Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India, (1996) 5 SCC 647, and M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, (1997) 2 SCC 353. The Court also relied on Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India, (1996) 5 SCC 281, for the need to reconcile development with ecological protection.

predicates.development_land_acquisition: An authority is acquiring land for development.
predicates.development_may_affect_ecology_or_enviro: The proposed development may affect ecology or the environment.

issues.definition: When land is acquired for development that may affect ecology or the environment, the authority must assess the effects beforehand and avoid grave ecological impairment.

issues.legal_issue: Environmental clearances required for an industrial project must be a mandatory condition of allotment rather than an advisory or discretionary request.
material_facts: The allotment letter asked the allottee to obtain necessary clearance from the pollution control board and the department responsible for ecology and environment, wherever applicable.
The Court considered that this wording left the clearance condition insufficiently mandatory and directed that clearances be required before allotment and before an industry was established.
issues.conclusion: The authority must make environmental clearance a mandatory condition for future project allotments, requiring clearance before the land is allotted.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the sustainable-development principle that industrial development must be reconciled with environmental protection. Articles 21, 48A and 51A(g) of the Constitution support that approach, as do Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India, (1996) 5 SCC 647, and M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, (1997) 2 SCC 353, including the precautionary principle.

predicates.industrial_project_allotment: An authority is allotting land for an industrial project.
predicates.environmental_clearance_condition_is_adv: The allotment terms merely request environmental clearance and do not make obtaining it mandatory before allotment.

issues.definition: When land is allotted for an industrial project under terms that make environmental clearance advisory, clearance must instead be a mandatory precondition to allotment.
